title: About Submarine Operations
text:
US submarines have played crucial roles in various conflicts throughout history, particularly during World War II. Their operations ranged from reconnaissance and intelligence gathering to direct combat engagements and support missions.

This guide covers the major types of submarine operations, tactical approaches, and the evolution of submarine warfare doctrine.
display_citation: Submarine Operations Guide — About Submarine Operations

title: War Patrols
text:
Combat patrols were the primary mission of WWII submarines. Boats patrolled assigned areas, hunting enemy shipping and naval vessels, and patrols typically lasted 30 to 60 days.

Key duties:

  • Ship and tanker hunting
  • Naval engagement
  • Commerce disruption
  • Area denial

title: Reconnaissance
text:
Submarines were ideal for covert reconnaissance missions, gathering intelligence on enemy positions, movements, and installations.

Key duties:

  • Beach reconnaissance for amphibious landings
  • Photo reconnaissance
  • Harbor surveillance
  • Weather reporting

title: Lifeguard Duty
text:
During air raids, submarines stationed near enemy territory rescued downed airmen from the water, saving hundreds of lives.

Key duties:

  • Stationed near bombing targets
  • Aircrew rescue operations
  • Surface ship rescue
  • Over 500 airmen saved in WWII

title: Supply and Transport
text:
Submarines transported supplies, personnel, and special forces to and from isolated or enemy-held areas.

Key duties:

  • Guerrilla support in the Philippines
  • Special forces insertion
  • Ammunition and supplies transport
  • Evacuations of key personnel
display_citation: Submarine Operations Guide — Supply and Transport

title: Mine Laying
text:
Some submarines were equipped to lay mines in enemy waters, creating hazards for enemy shipping lanes and harbors.

Key duties:

  • Harbor entrances
  • Shipping lanes
  • Strategic waterways
  • Covert deployment

title: Communication and Coordination
text:
Submarines served as radio relay stations and coordination platforms for multi-boat operations and intelligence gathering.

Key duties:

  • Wolf pack coordination
  • Radio relay
  • Intelligence transmission
  • Weather reporting
display_citation: Submarine Operations Guide — Communication and Coordination

title: Submerged Attack
text: The classic approach was a submerged attack using periscope observations, calculated firing solutions, and torpedo launches while avoiding detection.

title: Night Surface Attack
text: Particularly effective in the Pacific, submarines would surface at night to use their deck guns and higher speed for attacks and repositioning.
display_citation: Submarine Operations Guide — Night Surface Attack

title: Wolf Pack Tactics
text: Wolf pack tactics relied on coordinated attacks by multiple submarines, sharing intelligence and attacking convoys from multiple angles simultaneously.
display_citation: Submarine Operations Guide — Wolf Pack Tactics

title: Evasion and Escape
text: Evasion and escape depended on silent running, deep diving, use of thermal layers, and strict noise discipline to avoid depth charge attacks and enemy detection.
display_citation: Submarine Operations Guide — Evasion and Escape

title: WWII Pacific Theater Statistics
text:
Selected statistics highlighted in the operations guide:

  • 1,560 enemy ships sunk
  • 52 US submarines lost
  • 288 active submarines
  • 1,682 war patrols

US submarines accounted for approximately 55% of all Japanese shipping losses during WWII while representing only 2% of the US Navy.
